<reason>A won the central comparison between binding emissions performance and a common coal endpoint. B offered plausible investment-certainty and coordination benefits, but repeatedly treated A’s binding budgets as voluntary delay. A directly answered the first-mover questions: waiting would still require equivalent emissions reductions. A also used B’s concessions on gas replacement and infrastructure extensions to expose unresolved costs of the deadline. B never adequately explained why eliminating tightly emission-limited reserve plants delivers enough additional climate benefit to justify those costs.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>After B conceded that long-lived gas replacement could satisfy the agreement, A explained why “not required” misses the objection: a binding deadline can incentivize that compliant substitute when clean replacements arrive late. This connected the engineering objection directly to cumulative emissions rather than merely resisting coal retirement.</best_rebuttal>
